title: Bendigo Writers Festival offers 'unreserved' apology to author Abdel-Fattah
text:
The organisers of a disastrous 2025 Bendigo Writers Festival have apologised to author Randa Abdel-Fattah.

The Palestinian Australian academic launched legal action against Greater Bendigo City Council and event sponsor La Trobe University in June, claiming she was discriminated against on the basis of her political beliefs or activity.

On Friday, a joint statement from the council and university confirmed the legal dispute had been resolved.

Council chief executive Andrew Cooney apologised unreservedly to Dr Abdel-Fattah "for the harm the council caused to her".

"[The council] acknowledges and sincerely regrets that we infringed Dr Abdel-Fattah's intellectual and artistic freedom," the council statement said.

Andrew Cooney unreservedly apologised to Dr Abdel-Fattah. (Supplied: City of Greater Bendigo)

La Trobe University's Vice-Chancellor Theo Farrell also unreservedly apologised to the author.

"The university respects the importance of academic freedom and freedom of speech, and the need for respect of these powerful human rights," the statement said.

" The university has learned lessons from the 2025 Bendigo Writers Festival and will do better in the future. "

Dr Abdel-Fattah was due to speak at the August 2025 festival about her book, Discipline, when a code of conduct was sent to authors three days prior.

The 2025 Bendigo Writers Festival went ahead with a heavily reduced program. (ABC)

It included an expectation for speakers on La Trobe University's sponsored session, including Dr Abdel-Fattah, to comply with a contested Universities Australia definition of antisemitism.

Dr Abdel-Fattah withdrew from the festival and more than 50 other authors boycotted, leading to the cancellation of events, including the opening and closing nights.

"I accept the unreserved apologies as acknowledgement of the harm inflicted on me, my right to intellectual and artistic freedom and my human rights," Dr Abdel-Fattah said yesterday.

Clare Wright says staff and the other authors also deserve an apology.

'Staff were collateral damage'

Historian Clare Wright was a guest curator for the 2025 festival and was among those who boycotted the event. She shared the joint statement in a social media post yesterday.

"Would be nice if both institutions also unreservedly apologised to the staff who were collateral damage… and the 50+ authors who also pulled out of BWF, either in solidarity with Randa and/or because they themselves could not in all good conscience and practice sign the Code of Conduct," she wrote.

Ms Wright recently took a voluntary redundancy from La Trobe University.

Launching the legal action in June, Dr Abdel-Fattah said universities and cultural institutions must be held accountable for discrimination and anti-Palestinian racism.

"This is not a time for normalising the racism and repression demanded by the antisemitism definitions that are being used to silence those who speak out against Israel, an apartheid state and genocidal settler colony," she said.

Greater Bendigo City Council reviewed the 2025 writers festival and decided to take the year off in 2026, in part due to the "reputational damage incurred".

Plans for a 2027 festival are yet to be announced.

title: Snails cause harvest headache for South Australian farmers
text:
An abundance of snails is causing some farmers to lose money amid a harvest that is expected to break records.

On the Yorke Peninsula, fifth-generation farmer David Edwards is used to snails in his crop, but this year has been extreme.

"Nearly every paddock you look at, there's just hundreds, and hundreds, and hundreds," Mr Edwards said.

Snails have been seen covering entire fence posts. (Supplied: Lindsay Elliott)

Snails prefer alkaline soil, where they can access the calcium required to grow their shells. This soil type is prominent on the Yorke Peninsula.

When it comes time to harvest, the pests pose a number of challenges.

"You're only allowed about two per half litre at the silos, and when you've got thousands going into the machine, it's pretty hard to deliver grain without a lot of effort," Mr Edwards said.

"They're messy in the header, they're messy in augers, and it costs me a lot of money and a workman full time during harvest."

In extreme numbers, the snails cause a mess when it comes to harvest. (Supplied: David Edwards)

Before it gets to the silos, Mr Edwards's grain has been through two cleaning augers and a roller.

"It'd be an absolute delight to sit on the header and put ... the barley out of the header, or whatever, straight into a truck instead of going through three bins and four applications of different things to try to get rid of them."

The price of snails

At the silos, too many snails in a delivery can cause the grain to be downgraded, reducing the amount farmers are paid.

Mr Edwards has had one load of canola downgraded due to three snails.

At Cummins, Bruce Morgan sorted a big pile of snails out of 500 tonnes of canola. (Supplied: Bruce Morgan)

Grain receiver T-Ports' grower relations officer, Hayley Lewis, said there had been a "higher number of snails" this year, particularly from coastal growers such as those on the Eyre and Yorke peninsulas.

When the grain reaches the silos, samples are taken and tested, and the delivery is graded accordingly.

"For example, this year, the majority of the wheat is APW [Australian Premium White] or ASW [Australian Standard White]," Ms Lewis said.

"In a half-a-litre sample of wheat for grades H1 to ASW, there can only be one snail.

"If you exceed that one snail limit, the tolerance extends to 10 snails in a half-a-litre sample, but then you'll get downgraded to AGP [Australian General Purpose] quality."

At Minlaton on the Yorke Peninsula, some of David Edwards's crops have been downgraded at the silo due to snails. (Supplied: David Edwards)

While prices vary at sites, at the time of writing, APW1 wheat was priced at $330 per tonne in Wallaroo on the Yorke Peninsula, while the same processor priced AGP1 at $295.

South Australia produced 6.8 million tonnes of wheat in 2022-2023. Assuming all 4,500 grain farms in SA produced wheat, the total price difference between APW1 and AGP1 would equate to more than $50,000 per farm.

"We have had a couple of growers just happy to take whatever they can get because they know they have a snail issue, or they perhaps don't have access to a snail crusher," Ms Lewis said.

"Perhaps if they're at the tail end of their program, they're just happy to get it off and take whatever they can get. But others might take it home and put it through a snail crusher."

For Mr Edwards, the snails have been a downer for an otherwise record-breaking harvest.

"This is about my 57th harvest, and I reckon it is the best one I have ever, ever seen so far," he said.

title: North Melbourne AFLW duo announce retirement after historic three-peat
text:
Inaugural AFLW North Melbourne captain and eight-time All Australian Emma Kearney has announced her retirement following the Kangaroos' third straight premiership victory.

Kearney joined North Melbourne in 2019 after two years at the Western Bulldogs, where she also won a flag.

She led the Kangaroos for six seasons before handing over the captaincy to Jasmine Garner before the 2025 campaign, having steered the club to its maiden AFLW premiership in 2024.

Her teammate, three-time premiership player, inaugural player and long-time partner, Kate Shierlaw, also announced her retirement.

The pair told teammates today they would both be hanging up their boots.

(From left) Emma Kearney, Kangaroos coach Darren Crocker, and Kate Shierlaw, who says the third flag was the most emotional of the lot. (Getty: Morgan Hancock/AFL Photos)

“This club means the world to me, and I couldn’t be prouder of everything we’ve built and achieved together” Kearney said.

"Getting the opportunity to join North Melbourne ahead of our inaugural season in 2019 was so special, and watching this program grow into what it is today has been the greatest privilege of my career.

“The thing I’ll miss the most is simply being around this group every single day. Walking away from that daily environment is the hardest part.

“I’m so grateful to Crock (coach Darren Crocker) for the belief, guidance and care he has shown me and the entire group.

“Finally, a massive thank you to the North Melbourne fans. Your passion and loyalty through all the highs and lows has meant everything to us, and sharing these moments with you is something I’ll cherish forever.”

North Melbourne three-peat North Melbourne claims a historic three-peat after a near flawless but challenging season.

Following the premiership win over Melbourne last night at Princes Park, Crocker said Kearney had "left a legacy for our football club".

"She has really set the standards, when a lot of players actually didn't understand what it looked like," he told reporters post win.

Garner, who asked Kearney on stage to lift the cup beside her, said she was "an amazing player but also an amazing person".

"I looked up to her. A lot of us didn't really know what it looked like to have really high standards and work hard and be a team-first player," Garner said.

"I feel like she helped guide us through that.

"Not sure what she's going to do, but it was just really nice to have her up there (on stage)."

Shierlaw, an inaugural player for Carlton and co-captain for St Kilda before joining North, told ABC Sport the third flag was the most emotional win of the lot.

"I'm very overwhelmed with emotions. Relief, excited," Shierlaw said.

"It's just like a lot of hard work over four or five years … just Kearns and I having a great time out here, living our dreams. Three in a row."

title: MotoGP circuit to claim fewer trees as transplant solution offered
text:
South Australia's state government has reduced the number of trees to be removed for the controversial MotoGP circuit, with 94 olive trees to be "transplanted" across the Adelaide Park Lands.

The change means the total number of trees destroyed for the sporting event will be reduced to 288.

The olive trees are currently located between Wakefield Road and Bartels Road and will be transplanted to existing olive groves within the Park Lands.

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the project was worthy of pursuit, after seeking expert approval from arborists.

"That is a big difference to where we were previously," Mr Malinauskas said.

The state government says the species is 'hardy' and will have a high survival rate when transplanted. (ABC News)

The premier said arborists provided a "high confidence" the hardy species would have a "very high survival rate".

"Some can be transplanted quickly subject to the identified locations, but others will be put into temporary storage arrangements in pots", Mr Malinauskas said.

The reduction in tree casualties comes after a long-running feud between activists and the Malinauskas government and a call from dozens of celebrities to halt the tree removal.

Two legal challenges almost placed roadblocks in the way of the MotoGP circuit construction, but those challenges fell over in the Supreme and Federal courts.

The premier confirmed the olive tree transplanting work would start next month.

The state government said it engaged extensively with the Adelaide City Council before confirming a solution.

Protesters watch as trees in Adelaide's parklands are removed for the MotoGP circuit construction in November. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Adelaide City Council Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith welcomed the news, saying the olive trees had historical significance.

"They really have followed the path of settlement in South Australia," she said.

"Clearly it's technically difficult … but we understand it's possible and it can be done."

Adelaide Park Lands Association deputy president Tim Jackson described the government's move as a "small concession".

Mr Jackson said the premier was in "damage control" several days before major construction was due to begin.

"Tree loss is very, very significant. At the end of the day, this is a park, not a race track," he said.

The state government said that, including the olive trees, a total of 182 trees would be transplanted within the Park Lands.

New renders were released today to show which olive trees will be transplanted between Bartels and Wakefield roads.

The government released a new map in November 2026 to show which trees (in dark green) will be transplanted. (Supplied: SA Government)

Outside of the motorsport event period, the government said this section of the Park Lands would feature 124 mature trees in planter boxes to become a new tree-lined connection for people walking and cycling between the city and the eastern suburbs.

title: Culture preserved in new Aboriginal language dictionaries
text:
Two Aboriginal languages from Western Australia's Pilbara have been recorded and preserved in dictionaries for the first time, including one language with only three remaining fluent speakers.

The first drafts of the dictionaries were developed as part of a project by Puutu Kunti Kurrama and Pinikura (PKKP) Aboriginal Corporation to preserve Pinikura and Puutu Kunti Kurrama languages.

With both languages passed down through oral tradition, the dictionaries are the product of two years of collaboration between linguists and the remaining local speakers.

Pinikura traditional owner Terry Drage helped linguists with pronunciation.

"You can get a linguist to come in, and they will pronounce it their way," he said.

"And then that pronunciation, if we keep going with that type of pronunciation, then you lose [it]."

Terry (left) and Mitchell Drage believe the dictionaries could have an important role in the future. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

Terry's brother, elder Mitchell Drage, is also a big advocate of the project.

Only three people speak Pinikura fluently, and Mitchell Drage would like that to change.

" To me, it also says to the younger generation that our old people did have a language, and we need to maintain that as a record for the young people to hear. "

Writing an oral language

Linguist Breanna Kelly found documenting a language traditionally passed down orally one of the hardest parts of compiling the dictionary.

"A lot of the work that we do involves asking people questions to try and have them say some sentences back to us," she said.

"But we try to get information in different styles as much as we can, whether that's us just asking questions or whether it's more of a conversation, occasionally a bit of a role play."

Breanna Kelly hopes community members can use the dictionaries alongside online resources to learn the languages. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Ms Kelly said the team worked with present-day speakers and historical resources.

"It's been challenging but really fun," Ms Kelly said.

"I've enjoyed picking up little bits of language along the way."

PKKP launched Pinikura and Kurrama language dictionaries at its 2026 AGM. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

'It's our responsibility'

Burchell Hayes, a Puutu Kunti Kurrama descendant, said shame around getting the language wrong can be a barrier for younger Kurrama people wanting to learn it.

"We want them to identify themselves as Kurrama and be proud of who they are and be confident to be able to speak that language without that shame factor creeping in," Mr Hayes said.

He said it was why the first draft of the Kurrama dictionary is a good base, but not the final product.

Burchell Hayes says the release of the Kurrama dictionary is a proud moment. (ABC Pilbara: Kimberley Putland)

The next drafts of the dictionaries are already underway, with plans to improve on the first editions by gathering feedback from community members.

Terry Drage believes these first drafts have been a big first step.

"It's a legacy that's been handed down to us," he said.

"And now it's our responsibility to pass it on as well."

title: Workers who lose their jobs to AI say they're also addicted to using it
text:
Until a few months ago, Oksana had her pick of acting jobs in China.

The 26-year-old was booked back-to-back to work on short-drama projects, usually bite-sized serialised videos made specifically for mobile viewing.

But this year, that work has all but disappeared because of the rise of videos produced with artificial intelligence (AI).

"Many of the companies I used to know and work with have switched to AI and no longer shoot live-action dramas," she said.

"Now getting a role is very hard.

"If I wanted to, I previously could have kept shooting until I dropped dead.

" This year, that's no longer the case. The short drama industry is completely different. "

How fast has the shift happened?

In 2026, more than 90 per cent of China's new micro dramas were generated by AI, including the actors, voices and scenes.

They were nearly non-existent the year before.

Rather than a whole crew and set, micro dramas can be made by very small teams on computers in a studio. (ABC)

Government figures show about 1,600 new AI micro dramas launched every day for the first half of 2026.

The AI videos have become so popular that even someone like Oksana, who has lost her job to the technology, is "obsessed" with them.

"These AI dramas really are good, truly good," she said.

"With those two or 300-episode short dramas, once I click in, I forget about getting out.

"Even when I go to sleep each night, I leave the sound on and fall asleep listening.

"My head is a bit of a mess every day now, and I can't focus on anything else."

Micro dramas for macro audiences

The micro drama episodes often focus on fantasy, underdog-style or romantic storylines alongside time-travelling and urban dramas.

The episodes are usually free and end on cliffhangers designed to keep people watching, with viewers having to pay to see the rest of the series.

One of China's biggest hits of 2026, drawing 6.08 billion views, is a series where a woman wakes up in the Tang dynasty and gains power by slaying demons that roam the city.

AI-generated videos of pets and anthropomorphic fruit are also finding large audiences.

AI micro drama developer Zhu Zhili said the technology allowed companies to produce entertainment content quicker, cheaper and with more advanced storylines.

"Before, we needed to hire real actors, build sets, go into studios, and so on," he said.

Zhu Zhili says AI makes production much more efficient. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

"Now, with AI, we only need a very small team working together on computers in a company or studio to produce a short drama that previously would have taken enormous manpower and resources to shoot.

"We can just use AI to do the pictures, storyboard generation, generative audio, generative music, and generative voiceover.

"So the efficiency is very, very high now."

AI creators have reported dramas may cost about one-tenth of traditional live-action shoots.

But Mr Zhu said despite the large volume of new dramas being made, turning a profit could still be difficult.

"In the first half of this year, China produced a total of 220,000 AI short dramas, which is an enormous number," he said.

"But on the other hand, only about 1,000 of them truly broke out, meaning they succeeded, passed 100 million views, or made money, a share of less than 0.4 per cent."

Zhu Zhili uses AI for pictures, storyboarding and generative audio, music and voiceover. (ABC News: Allyson Horn)

China has ambitious goals to have AI agents, devices and applications reach 90 per cent penetration in key sectors by 2030.

The government's current five-year plan also lists micro dramas as an emerging form of "cultural business" to be actively developed.

The AI entertainment industry's development has moved at breakneck speed since the release of powerful new AI video software, like tech group ByteDance's Seedance 2.0 model.

But Chinese social media is full of stories and complaints by former actors who are now out of work.

"Then this year, after AI became widespread, nearly all my peers stopped getting call sheets. I've been at home without work for several months too," said user Liu Yuzhan, who now works as a delivery driver.

Oksana admits she is addicted to the micro dramas herself. (ABC)

Oksana says it's a similar story among her industry friends, but she believes there will always be an appetite for real human acting in longer-form content.

"Many of my peers have switched to livestreaming because of the current environment and can no longer work as professional actors," she said.

"But AI content gets tiresome if you watch it for long.

"It can never replace live actors, or the imperfections in their acting and their subtle emotions.

"AI is formulaic and can't convey emotion."

title: The tactics that secured North Melbourne's third AFLW premiership
text:
As rain bucketed down, North Melbourne confirmed its AFLW dynasty with an historic third consecutive premiership.

While it may seem repetitive to talk about the Roos' record-breaking run, what they had to compete with in 2026 makes this third flag that little bit more special.

For the first time since 2023 they lost a game, and challengers consistently came closer than in the previous two years.

The looming feeling that senior players could potentially hang up their boots also added a sense of occasion to the victory.

And then the weather showed up. The rain was going to be the great equaliser, allowing fellow grand finalist Melbourne to gather some confidence.

But by dominating three specific phases of the game, North Melbourne made history on Friday night, securing a three-peat.

The fast start that set up the victory

Throughout 2026, North Melbourne hasn't been an overly strong first-quarter team.

Generally, the opening terms were largely arm wrestles, almost like the Roos were playing with the opposition, giving them hope, before taking it away.

Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season North Melbourne claims a historic three-peat after a near flawless but challenging season.

But on Friday night, the fast start was necessary. With rain already falling, and more on the radar, any early lead was going to be seriously valuable, so the Roos ensured they were the team in front.

Tess Craven knocked through the first goal of the game within 21 seconds, and captain Jasmine Garner kicked a second six minutes in. They went direct, gained ground with kicks, and got deep entries to unsettle Melbourne's typically staunch defence.

Both goals for the Roos came from stoppage, which was a worrying sign for Melbourne so early on. Last time these sides met, it was off turnover — not stoppage — that North Melbourne had set itself apart.

But this time around, the Roos tipped those scales in their favour.

Score sources North Melbourne Melbourne Points from intercept 15 13 Points from stoppage 29 5

Best on ground medallist Garner set the tone early in the piece. In the first quarter alone, Garner's stats included seven disposals, four inside 50s, and the goal, laying the foundations for how North Melbourne was going to attack the game.

While it took Melbourne some time to adapt to what the game was throwing up, North Melbourne just got to work.

The Demons over-possessed the footy in slippery conditions, opting for the handball too often, instead of getting boot to ball to win all-important territory.

Holding steady as the Dees fought back

Once Melbourne managed to get into the game, the Roos had to simply batten down the hatches and absorb the blows being thrown their way.

But crucially, just as in the first quarter, North Melbourne had already taken advantage of its early momentum on the scoreboard, with a classy Eilish Sheerin goal 39 seconds into the next term.

The Demons shifted to more of a kicking game in the second quarter, got into more dangerous positions, and Tayla Harris's contested marking reared its head. With this shift, they kicked what would be their only two goals of the match.

That shift in style was borne out in the stats, with Melbourne's ratio of 39 kicks to 14 handballs in the second quarter helping to throw North Melbourne's movement out of whack.

While the second quarter was Melbourne's lowest-disposal quarter of the match, it was the side's most effective. Notably, both of the goals came from intercepts.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

Pressure was also a major consideration in the second term, with Melbourne recording a pressure factor of 2.30 across the quarter — a rate at the upper end of the elite category — which rose to 2.38 in the third term.

But, crucially for the Roos, they maintained a lead even when the Demons threw their best at them. And the third quarter became a stalemate, in which North Melbourne maintained its arm's-length lead. The Roos' deep defence was staunch, repelling repeated forward entries and preventing Melbourne from scoring further goals.

Midfielders Garner (eight intercepts) and Ash Riddell (seven) were important in this respect, sliding behind the ball post-stoppage, while winger Amy Gavin Mangan, half-forward Jenna Bruton, and half-back Eliza Shannon (all six intercepts) got busy defensively.

In doing so, they lulled the Demons back into over-possession of the footy, taking their kick rate way back down to 50 per cent.

Essentially, the middle two quarters were a tale of the Roos just taking the hits and remaining on their feet.

Five-minute burst seals the premiership

While the game largely felt like it was in the balance for the duration, a five-minute patch in the last quarter turned a six-point lead into a 26-point victory for North Melbourne. It was a classic demonstration of the Roos' brand, taking the game away in a flash.

Melbourne controlled territory for the bulk of that term, attempting to break through the numbers in its attacking arc but unable to convert for the major that would have really rattled the Roos.

Instead, North Melbourne again absorbed the blows — and then the fast break happened. A long rebounding kick unlocked the Roos' speed, which had been a worry for Melbourne all evening and in the end proved the difference.

It allowed the Roos to set up an attack once again, create a stoppage inside 50, and secure a crucial goal off the boot of Bella Eddey.

And that goal was the dam wall breaking. It put the Roos up by 13 points, and opened the floodgates for two more goals via Blaithin Bogue, taking the game from a thrilling nailbiter to a comprehensive North Melbourne victory.

This is the Roos' style: absorb, absorb, absorb — then land the felling blow.

Throughout the season they have consistently dominated late in games.

They kicked the last three goals in their preliminary final, and continued the trend by kicking the last three goals in the grand final.

Prior to the game, one question for Melbourne was whether it could prevent that final flurry and hold on.

On Friday night, North Melbourne provided an emphatic answer.

title: Adelaide-born WWE wrestler Bronson Reed dies at 38
text:
Wrestling authorities have paid tribute to Adelaide-born wrestler Jermaine Haley, also known as Bronson Reed, who has died at the age of 38.

World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) attributed Haley's death to medical complications.

"Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague," WWE said in a statement.

" Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jermaine's entire family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, their daughter, as well as his friends, co-workers and fans. "

Fellow Adelaide WWE wrestler Demiti Bennett, whose ring name is Rhea Ripley, posted a photo of herself and Haley on Instagram with the caption: "I love you bro. Shattered."

During an appearance on the ABC's Summer Grandstand in October last year, Haley told the podcast that while growing up in Adelaide, he would wrestle with mates in his living room and backyard.

"For me, [a] long-time wrestling fan, I've watched every generation of WWE," Haley said at the time.

As Bronson Reed, Haley was known as a villain or "heel" in the WWE sport, telling the ABC that crowd booing would help fuel his performances.

"I love the boos," he said. "The thing is, however the [crowd is] reacting — whether they're cheering or booing — they're making noise.

"If you're someone [who] can invoke that from the people, then you're doing that well."

title: No end in sight to three-year dispute between outback council and their only GP
text:
A funding dispute over an isolated West Australian town's only medical practice highlights the broader health funding gap facing rural communities, with a new report calling for a $250,000 annual Commonwealth payment to help keep small-town GP services running.

The Shire of Dundas and veteran GP Graham Rowlands have been locked in a dispute over the funding of his practice in Norseman, 630 kilometres east of Perth, for more than three years.

The Local Government Rural Health Funding Alliance's (LGRHFA) November research paper says small and remote communities often lack the patient numbers to cover the fixed costs of running a general practice, leaving councils to subsidise services.

Regional development consultant Caroline Robinson, whose firm 150Square helped prepare the report, said higher Medicare bulk-billing incentives for remote doctors were not enough.

"The Medicare bulk billing does not cover the floor costs for a general practice," she said.

Caroline Robinson says Medicare bulk billing is not keeping up with inflation. (Supplied)

The report proposes a $250,000 annual Commonwealth payment towards those costs for eligible practices in small, remote communities.

Ms Robinson said the issue was not simply a shortage of doctors.

"It's not a workforce supply issue. It costs more to deliver a general practice in the regions," she says.

Norseman: a local example

The Shire of Dundas has been part of discussions around the LGRHFA's work, with its ongoing disagreement with Dr Rowlands illustrating the pressures facing small communities.

Dr Rowlands says the proposed $250,000 annual Commonwealth payment would help, but he would still need additional support from the shire to make the practice sustainable, estimating the total annual payment at about $400,000, plus housing, a vehicle and locum support.

The shire and Dr Rowlands have disagreed over the financial support needed to keep his practice operating, with their previous agreement ending in October 2023.

Dr Rowlands said his Norseman practice has remained open since 2023, apart from about two weeks when he took leave, and that he offered the shire a locum to cover.

At a heated public meeting on November 22 to discuss medical services for the town, shire president Laurene Bonza alleged Dr Rowlands had charged unauthorised fuel and grocery purchases to the shire.

Laurene Bonza says she wanted everybody to understand the shire's perspective in relation to its relationship with the doctor and how has broken down. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

Dr Rowlands was not at the meeting but told the ABC he denies the allegations, saying a written agreement allowed him to use shire funds for fuel for his personal and shire vehicles.

Cr Bonza said the council wanted to secure an ongoing medical service and needed to plan for Dr Rowlands's eventual departure.

"With the best will in the world, he's not going to be here forever," she says.

"It's going to be difficult to get another doctor, which is why we want to know when he's planning to leave to give us a lead time to put things in place so that we do have a doctor."

Dr Rowlands said small bulk-billing practices in towns like Norseman needed financial support to remain viable.

He said he remained willing to supply ongoing medical services but wanted future discussions with the shire to involve a neutral third party, which was proposed at the meeting.

"I'm happy to support the population, and I'm happy to facilitate in any way an ongoing health service to the Norseman community," Dr Rowlands said.

Police were present throughout the community meeting in Norseman. (ABC Goldfields: Daniel Holmes)

Norseman hotelier Therese Wade says losing the town's doctor could have consequences beyond healthcare.

"Without a doctor you'd probably lose the hospital, become a nursing post, you'd definitely lose the chemist," she says.

Resident Alys McDonough said common sense is not being followed by community leaders making these decisions.

"There's also a cost being put on these sorts of things; how much does a human life cost really?" she says.

Calls for Commonwealth support

Caroline Robinson said councils could not sustainably fund medical services at the expense of other responsibilities, with some foregoing spending on roads and housing.

"The Commonwealth could play in this thin market space so that local governments can return their rates to their core business," she said.

The LGRHFA wants its proposed payment considered during discussions around the National Health Reform Agreement.

The federal government says it is investing in more doctors and nurses for rural communities, including higher bulk-billing incentives and a $49.76 million commitment to the General Practice Incentive Fund.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing says engagement with the Primary Health Network and WA Health has not identified Norseman as a priority location for this fund.

The state government said primary care remained a Commonwealth responsibility.

But a spokesperson pointed to the training of 20 additional rural generalist doctors through the WA Country Health Service, and said its advocacy to the federal government remained ongoing.

title: Mixed emotions as buffel grass not named weed of national significance
text:
A fast-spreading invasive weed that can destroy animal habitats and choke native plants has been spared a listing as a weed of national significance after fierce debate between the cattle industry, Indigenous land managers and environmental groups.

Stakeholders were alerted on Friday afternoon of the National Biosecurity Committee's (NBC) decision not to list buffel as a national weed priority, which prevents nationally coordinated efforts to control the weed.

Romy Carey says the decision not to list buffel grass as a weed of national significance is a relief to pastoralists. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

First introduced by Afghan cameleers, it was in the 1960s that buffel was intentionally spread to control soil erosion and feed cattle — it is now present across Australia.

The fire-fuelling species is drought-resistant and was declared a weed in the Northern Territory in 2024.

However, pastoralists say buffel plays an important role as a cattle feed and that a national weed listing could impact their industry.

There are major efforts across Central Australia to control the spread of buffel. (ABC News: Ryan Liddle)

In a statement on its website, the NBC said due to a divergence of stakeholder views on the handling of buffel, and actions already taken in some jurisdictions, "NBC has not reached national consensus for it to be included as part of the ... initiative".

"Buffel grass presents a unique and complex case that required further consideration because it is a highly valued pasture grass (production asset) and causes harm (significant negative impacts) in some places, such as in conservation areas," the statement said.

Cattle industry relieved

Chief executive of the Northern Territory Cattlemen's Association, Romy Carey, said the decision not to list buffel was "welcome news" and a win for the cattle industry.

"This is a species of pasture that our cattle producers here in the territory and right across Australia rely on to feed our livestock," she said.

" To have the threat looming over with the declaration of a weed is just something that we are glad is now over, and we're looking forward to moving on with this. "

Romy Carey is the head of the NT Cattlemen's Association. (ABC: News Dane Hirst )

Ms Carey acknowledged buffel could be a risk to the environment but that the industry was "at the table and having those discussions".

"We recognise that there is a need to control it and we support action being taken where it's needed," she said.

She added that without the grass, the territory's cattle industry would not be what it is today.

Call for federal inquiry

The threat of buffel is a continuing concern of environmental groups and Indigenous land managers — who say they have seen the devastating impact of the grass firsthand.

The Invasive Species Council's Taigen Ryan said the decision exposed a failure in Australia's biosecurity system that allowed vested interests to take precedence over the environment.

Taigen Ryan says there must be a federal inquiry into the impact of buffel grass on the environment. (Supplied)

Ms Ryan said the listing would have facilitated national coordination and would not have taken away its use from pastoralists.

"It spreads, it infests, it kills, it chokes out everything else around it," she said.

However, she said she was not surprised by the decision.

Buffel grass spreads fast and burns hot, but has been used to control soil erosion for decades. (ABC Landline: Cameron Lang)

Ms Ryan called on the federal government to establish an inquiry into the country's inadequate response to the growing crisis.

"Now we need our federal leaders to actually do something about this, not be concerned or benign, not be concerned about their next election cycle, but be concerned about the legacy that they are leaving for future generations.

"[And] more importantly what they're leaving for country, because there is no more time for what is based on feelings."

Her call has been echoed by the Arid Land Environment Centre and the Central Land Council (CLC).

Garth Forrester says buffel grass is a threat to culture, health and infrastructure. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

CLC Indigenous land manager Garth Forrester said without a coordinated national approach to managing the weed, resources meant for looking after people on their country would be used for weed control instead.

"I do feel that the general public of Australia need to be informed on how this came about, how the decision was knocked back," he said.

"Buffel grass, it ticked all the boxes [for being listed].

title: Peter Cain resigns from Canberra Liberals
text:
Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain has resigned from the party to sit as an independent in the ACT Legislative Assembly.

In a statement, Mr Cain said he would be better placed to push for greater government transparency, responsible spending, and improved essential services from the crossbench.

He said his "values have not changed", adding that "what is changing is the freedom with which I can act upon them".

"The growing distance between what this government promises, what it spends and what it delivers should concern every Canberran," he said.

" I believe I can pursue these issues more effectively and freely as an Independent. "

Speaking to ABC Radio Canberra, he said he had been thinking about becoming an independent "for a little while".

He said there were "occasions when I thought, 'Gee, more could have been done with that', and it will be an opportunity now to do what I think serves the best interests of those people that reach out to me".

Mr Cain said he would recontest the 2028 election as an Independent. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

Mr Cain represents the electorate of Ginninderra, in north-west Canberra, and was elected to the Legislative Assembly in 2020.

In June 2025, Mr Cain resigned from the shadow cabinet, citing concerns about the party's leadership.

At the time he held the shadow ministries of attorney-general, planning and housing services.

In October last year he was suspended from the party room, alongside former leader Elizabeth Lee, for crossing the floor in the Legislative Assembly over moves to reduce the sitting calendar from 13 weeks to 12 in 2026.

Peter Cain resigns from Canberra Liberals shadow cabinet Canberra Liberals MLA Peter Cain resigns from the shadow cabinet, citing concerns about the party's leadership.

In December, Mr Cain returned to shadow cabinet, taking on the responsibilities of Government Services, Community Services and Disability, Veterans, and Seniors.

He added City Services to his list of portfolios earlier this year, following the resignation of former leader Leanne Castley.

Mr Cain's resignation from the Canberra Liberals today means the opposition will have seven seats in the Legislative Assembly. The crossbench will have eight seats.

He is the second Liberal to quit the party room this year and become an independent, following Ms Castley's resignation in June.

Mr Cain said Belconnen would "remain at the heart of his parliamentary work".

He said the "risks are real and obviously any parliamentarian would think about where they're best placed to achieve their goals, but my goals are actually to make Belconnen a really successful and well-serviced district".

Mr Cain has confirmed he will recontest Ginniderra as an independent at the next territory election in 2028.

'Came as a surprise'

The Canberra Liberals said they were "disappointed" by Mr Cain's decision to leave the party.

"The people of Ginninderra voted for a Canberra Liberal, and that is the mandate on which he was elected on," they wrote in a statement.

"Peter's decision came as a surprise, and it says more about Peter than it does about the Canberra Liberals."

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton said he "really [didn't] understand" what led to Peter's decision and said it was "disheartening".

Canberra Liberals leader Mark Parton says the Canberra Liberals are disappointed in Peter Cain's decision to leave the party. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

Mr Parton said he was only told about Mr Cain's decision late on Friday night when the party received an email from Mr Cain asking to rescind his party membership.

The leader said he had since spoken to Mr Cain to express his disappointment.

Mr Parton said Mr Cain had "raised some concerns" with him a week ago.

"It certainly wasn't done in the manner of someone who was seeking to leave the party," Mr Parton said.

The party said his resignation "gives us the chance to refresh our representation in Ginninderra", adding that they would put forward candidates "who would be ready to fight" at the next election.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr said the government would work "constructively with Mr Cain in his role on the crossbench".

Trainer Rob Archibald said the addition of blinkers played a key role for Cristal Clear after he won the group 3 Festival Stakes (1500m) to join his team for the $2 million Ingham (1600m) in two weeks at Randwick. A $26 chance on Saturday at Rosehill after finishing four lengths back in the Ladies Day Cup (1500m) last start at Hawkesbury, Cristal Clear was taken to the lead by Jason Collett then kicked and fought off Sun God late to win by half a length. Cristal Clear, left, kicks late to take out the Festival Stakes. Getty Images Archibald, who trains in partnership with wife, Annabel, said the five-year-old, which won the group 2 Ajax Stakes in March, was now headed to the Ingham with stablemate and Gong runner-up Formal Display. He said Big Dance winner Hellsing could also go there if he pleases in the two weeks, following a disappointing run in the Gong. Ciaron Maher assistant trainer Johann Gerard-Dubord said Gong winner Gringotts was now likely to continue on to the Ingham.

Advertisement

As for the turnaround from Cristal Clear on Saturday, Archibald said: “Obviously, blinkers back on and maybe just a bit of give in the track. “It might have been just the set-up, and I think the ride, with positive intent up on speed, I think that obviously helps. He is very good.” The win gave the Archibalds and Collett a double on the day. Collett won the Country Classic on Stephen and Jordan Lee-trained Giapponese, while Sacrify saluted earlier at $13 for the Archibalds. The stable was unlucky when Wootton Lass was held up badly when third. “That was a tough one, but it’s been a good day,” Archibald said. The Maher stable claimed the listed ATC Cup (2000m) with Paltrow Miss in the next. Ash Morgan took the $3.20 chance to just off the leaders from gate 13, and she was strong late to hold out Imperalist by half a length after hitting the front at the 300m mark.

Advertisement

Gerard-Dubord said the mare, now with a first stakes win, would likely chase similar races in Sydney. Secret’s out after Starlight win Trainer Joe Pride was considering a shot at the Razor Sharp in two weeks, and planning on much better races in the autumn, with King’s Secret after the five-year-old defied the market to edge out $1.65 favourite Roselyn’s Star in the listed Starlight Stakes (1100m). Freshened up after a disappointing 12th in the $2 million Sydney Stakes (1200m), King’s Secret was taken from the outside gate to race outside leader Arriving Home by Andrew Adkins before the $12 chance nosed out Roselyn’s Star in an epic battle to the line. Pride was in disbelief at the gap between King’s Secret and Roselyn’s Star in the market given his horse had raced admirably in Everest lead-up races, including a neck third to Mazu in The Shorts.

Advertisement

“The market normally gets it right,” Pride said. “On this occasion, they got it wrong, so pay the believers.” King’s Secret, left carrying the green and black colours, beats Roselyn’s Star. Getty Images The Warwick Farm trainer was now focusing on more 1100m races with King’s Secret, which recorded his sixth at the trip. “There’s the Razor Sharp in a couple weeks, but I’ll just see how he pulls up,” he said.

Advertisement

“I’m just so happy to see him do that. The preparation so far had been winless, and I hate good horses going winless through a prep. “He raced against the top company and look, to be fair to him, he probably isn’t up to those horses at the moment. Clearly he isn’t, but that’s not saying we won’t get there in 12 months. “The last run was so disappointing, so I just said, ‘Guys, it’s a long time to the autumn if I tip him out now. Let’s just give me a couple weeks off, bring him back for this.’ “To me, it was about a bit of fact finding and I think I’ve got a few answers.” He also had high praise for the ride of Adkins.

Advertisement

“He took his time, he didn’t just rush him across, and then when the speed slowed up a bit, Zac [Lloyd] had to pull out and actually go three wide on Roselyn’s Star, and he ended up probably with the worst run in transit than we did, and all the punters were just of the belief that that was going to be the opposite. “I mean, how do they bet on maps? I go off the horses, and there’s not much between those two horses.” Perfect storm brewing for flying filly Adrian Bott was eyeing the Storm Boy path for Infallible after the Hellbent filly scored an impressive debut in the 1100m two-year-old handicap. The $180,000 buy, which won both of her trials, flew out of the gates to lead easily under Tim Clark before maintaining a margin over $1.5 million colt River Of Rome, a full brother to Beadman, for a two and a quarter-length win.

Advertisement

Infallible was in from $34 (TAB) to equal Golden Slipper favourite at $15 with Soldi. Stablemate and Breeders’ Plate winner Flying Houdini was $17. Bott said Flying Houdini was back in work and at this stage the Blue Diamond was a likely first target, rather than the Inglis Millennium on February 6. He said Infallible would likely head to the BJ McLachlan Stakes (1200m) at Eagle Farm on Boxing Day as a lead-in to the $3 million Magic Millions Classic (1200m). Bott and co-trainer Gai Waterhouse-trained Storm Boy won the same Saturday race at Rosehill in 2023 before claiming that Queensland double. “She’s a good, tough little filly,” Bott said. “She’s a professional filly with natural speed and there’s a bit of substance there. “Physically, she’s the type that can handle a two-year-old campaign. There’s scope and upside to her and a lot of strength to get her through.”

Advertisement

Chris Waller-trained Fireball won the same Rosehill race last year before going on to take out the Inglis Millennium and group 1 Champagne Stakes. Randwick trainer John Thompson believes La Morra is a stayer in the making after winning the 2000m Midway Handicap despite a slow start and wide run early. The four-year-old mare, a $120,000 yearling buy for Thompson, was tough late to hold out Bearings by three-quarters of a length for a first city win. Thompson praised the poise of jockey Zac Lloyd after the early setbacks and the effort of the Toronado mare, which is named after a hilltop municipality in north-west Italy known for producing Nebbiolo wine. Lloyd leads the Sydney premiership on 42, four ahead of James McDonald, who won the Highway Handicap on Matt Dunn-trained Another Cashie and the last on Matt Smith’s Maybe Moet.

Advertisement

Mollie Fitzgerald edged ahead in the apprentices’ title with victory on Sacrify in the 1800m benchmark 78. Fitzgerald went to eight for the season, one up on defending champion Siena Grima. Sacrify, second-up on Saturday off a strong finish when sixth at Newcastle, won an identical race at Rosehill in July. Fitzgerald and the Archibalds were then unlucky in the next when Wootton Lass finished third in the 1400m benchmark 78 for fillies and mares. The $21 chance finished a length third behind Nacim Dilmi-trained Probability Theory, with Kris Lees’ Beneath The Rock in second. Wootton Lass looked likely to challenge before being pocketed behind leader Rose Aye at the 250m mark by Tommy Berry on Probability Theory. Berry was questioned about the shift in but escaped suspension. Dilmi, who trains the Domeland team at Wyong, said the Belle Of The Turf at Gosford on December 29 shaped as a likely next target for Probability Theory. The $300,000 Gateway at Eagle Farm on December 12 was another option.

Advertisement

Ballina trainer Stephen Lee was eyeing another shot at the group 3 Chairman’s Handicap (2000m) at Doomben after Giapponese made the most of a rails run from gate one to claim the Country Classic (2000m). Giapponese, named after the Italian word for Japanese, was having his 11th run of the preparation and first go at 2000m when Jason Collett took him to three-quarter length win over $101 shot Southern Dancer. Tyler Schiller had made a bold move around the field to the front on Southern Dancer approaching the turn. Lee, who trains in partnership with his son, Jordan, said he won the Chairman’s Handicap in 2018 with 150-1 shot Anton En Avant and he may take Giapponese to the same race next preparation.

A young buyer from Geelong is on the move after holding off her rivals for a historic apartment in a former theatre in Fitzroy. She was one of three bidders who contested 11/19 Victoria Street, helping it to skip past the $995,000 reserve, selling at auction for $1.2 million. The property was one of 629 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week. The buyer of the Fitzroy home had previously lived locally and was moving back to Melbourne from Geelong for work commitments, Jellis Craig Fitzroy agent and auctioneer Charles Atkins said.

A two-storey art deco East Lindfield home passed in at auction with a vendor’s bid of $3.2 million on Saturday. Staff from real estate agency DiJones almost outnumbered bidders and onlookers as they stood in the front garden of 82 Tryon Road, with both registered bidders arriving just minutes before the auction for the four-bedroom property began. The property was one of 1073 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 42 per cent from 637 reported results throughout the week, while 278 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. After extolling its original features spanning patterned ceilings, sandstone paving, and a curved stairwell with metal balustrade, auctioneer Josh Larsen opened bidding on the East Lindfield home.

Advertisement

Despite several conversations among sales agents and bidders, no one could be convinced to place a bid. After 10 minutes, the property passed in and the auction ended. Related Article Property prices The most liveable, affordable suburbs for property buyers At the time of publication, the property, which had a guide of $3 million and a reserve of $3.4 million, had not sold. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The house, which has covered terraces, parking for two cars and a studio space on the lower ground floor, was offered for the first time in more than 35 years.

Advertisement

Record show it last sold in 1991 for $470,000. It was the vendors’ family home, but they have held it as an investment since moving to the north coast. There was plenty of room to move at the auction of 82 Tryon Road, but it was not enough to entice bidders to raise their paddles. Sitthixay Ditthavong Larsen said while he had seen an uptick in transactions in the past eight weeks, the result reflected ongoing hesitation among buyers. “We have two very interested parties here, and we are trying to see what we can do,” he said. “We are seeing some engagement, but buyers are cautious.” The house still has many of its original features including patterned ceilings and a double archway leading to french doors. Domain

Advertisement

Earlier in the week, sales agent for DiJones, Nahid Coventry was anticipating strong interest from three parties, but only two showed up on the day, with buyers “hedging their bets” in the current market. “People are nervous,” she said. “They are still waiting to see rock bottom. Everyone is out for a bargain.” In Balmain, a three-storey, four-bedroom home sold for $4,402,000 at auction on Saturday, $352,000 over the reserve to a family from Ryde. Six parties registered to bid for 26 Birchgrove Road, with four active. Bidding opened at $3.75 million, $25,000 below the $4 million guide. The property called “Riverview” has scenic water views alongside a split-level garden deck and pool.

Advertisement

After the first couple of bids of $25,000 increments, the increments then jumped around from $5000 to $10,000 to $1000 bids. In the final moments it got down to increments of $1000 and $500, before the hammer fell and the property sold. It had a reserve of $4,050,000. The successful bidders were a family with teenagers from Ryde who were not present, but had a buyer’s agent acting on their behalf. They were attracted by the two living areas and swimming pool the house offered. The underbidders were an inner west family with three young children, while the vendors were relocating to Melbourne. A family from Ryde are all set for summer with the purchase of a four-bedroom home in Balmain. Domain

Advertisement

Belle Property Balmain sales agent, Monique Dower, said the house was last renovated about 16 years ago but had been refreshed ahead of the sale. “A lot of money was spent on the presentation to bring it up to a certain standard, including new carpets, new floors and a garden upgrade”. Records show the home last sold in 2008 for $1,535,000. Related Article Housing affordability Why the property downturn hasn’t made it much easier to buy a home In Sylvania, a single level, four-bedroom home sold for $2,155,000 to a couple from Zetland who paid $45,000 below reserve. They were moving to be closer to family.

Advertisement

Ten parties registered to vie for the keys to 21 Endeavour Street, with four active. Bidding opened with an offer of $1.9 million, followed by two further increments of $50,000. When bidding reached $2.1 million, which was also the guide, activity stalled. Sales agent for McGrath Sylvania, Bill Tsounias, then negotiated with the leading bidder to increase their offer to $2,155,000 and the hammer fell. The property had a reserve of $2.2 million. 21 Endeavour Street comes complete with a pool and cabana, ready for summer. Domain

Advertisement

The underbidders were a couple from Beverley Park who had sold their home last weekend. The vendors were taking advantage of market conditions to buy a larger home. Tsounias said the turnkey nature of the property was appealing to buyers, but not enough for most to raise their paddles. “[Results like this] clearly show that [you can have] 10 bidders but the second you hit the price guide, you have two bidders,” he said. “You tell them exactly where [the pricing] will be, and they still rock up thinking it might go for well under.”

Unheralded German Nicolai Von Dellingshausen has a Ryder Cup winner snapping at his heels as he eyes the biggest victory of his career at the Australian PGA and a potential major championship debut. In windy conditions that blew Von Dellinghausen’s playing partner Cameron Smith off course at The Lakes Golf Club in Sydney, the world No.333 took a three-shot lead through 54 holes at 16 under par. Nicolai Von Dellingshausen tees off at the Australian PGA Championship on Saturday. Getty Images Von Dellingshausen carded a gutsy 69 and continued to upstage several big names including Smith, Adam Scott and Min Woo Lee. In their place, 12-time DP World Tour winner and world No.25 Alex Noren threw his hat into the ring with a bogey-free 65 to climb to outright second at 13 under par.

Advertisement

“I’m extremely happy about the last two days,” world No.25 Noren, a member of Europe’s 2018 Ryder Cup-winning team, said after seven birdies on day three. “[The Lakes] varies and gives you opportunities when you have to step up. I took care of the par 5s and then you can play some of the other holes a little bit more defensively. It’s a really fun course to play.” Noren and Von Dellingshausen will comprise the final group on Sunday, teeing off at 12.15pm. Sweden’s Alex Noren moved into second place on Saturday. Getty Images Two-time Australian PGA champion Scott climbed to nine under with a bogey-free 65 that included an eagle at the par-5 eighth. At seven shots behind the lead, former world No.1 Scott gave himself a green light for an aggressive final round on Sunday. “I think I should, because what difference does it make?” Scott said. “I’m really in a fortunate position. I think I’ve won [it] twice before, so it’s not like I’m protecting anything. I should just have a crack.”

Advertisement

In front of large Sydney galleries cheering on Smith, the 2022 British Open winner struggled in the breeze to a two-over 74 that dropped his total to seven under. The third member of the group, Northern Ireland’s Tom McKibbin, missed a short birdie putt on the 17th but a solid 70 kept him within four shots of the lead. Off day: Cameron Smith. Getty Images Von Dellingshausen said he would spend the night either at his accommodation in Coogee with his wife and children, or exploring the Opera House with his mind coach to distract himself from what is at stake at the $2.5 million Australian PGA. The winner will be awarded a DP World Tour card for two years and more than $400,000 in prizemoney. But another significant carrot dangling is that, for the first time, the Australian PGA champion will receive a direct invitation to the US PGA Championship next year, one of golf’s four majors. “Yes, [winning] would [secure] my first major, which would be a huge thing,” Von Dellingshausen said. “At the same time, what I want to do is after the round, just look in the mirror and say, ‘Hey, I gave it my all and whatever happened, happened.’”

Jack Clayton offers a chuckle and wry smile when asked to recall the moment which paved his way towards earning his Baggy Green. Cricket was not a career path he envisioned when the Brisbane Lions academy prospect pondered what missing selection in the AFL draft would mean. When he picked up the bat for the University of Queensland, he was playing third-grade and was reluctant to give up his Saturday mornings when a request to be promoted to the seconds was offered. Queensland’s Jack Clayton celebrating a Sheffield Shield century at the Gabba. Chris Hyde/Getty Images Nine years to the day when he went un-drafted, and he is on the cusp of becoming Australia’s 474th Test cricketer, having been named in the squad to face New Zealand in Perth from December 9. “I certainly never thought when I gave up my footy dream that I would be in this position nine years later. At that stage, I did think I was going to go back and play footy for that season,” Clayton said on Saturday.

Test cricket Power rankings: The quicks and spinners primed to succeed all-star Test attack “The next season, Scott Henry – our first-grade captain, who also played for New South Wales and Queensland – told me I was going to bat three for the season, and I fell flat on my face when he said that. It’s obviously been a bit of a different journey, but one I’m really proud of.” That call-up marked a sliding doors moment for Clayton, who had initially intended to attempt an AFL revival mission through the NEAFL – now the VFL – with Aspley Hornets. “I think being out of that professional set-up with footy … and just being a normal 18, 19, 20-year-old going through uni, hanging out with mates, doing all the things uni people do, gave me a lot of perspective about life, but also where sport lies in my life,” he said. “I feel like that’s helped keep me balanced and level throughout my cricket career.”

While fellow Test contenders Sam Konstas and Jake Weatherald have fought for re-inclusion in the spotlight, Clayton has been able to slowly hone his craft free of scrutiny. In an era where T20 cricket and the smash and bash mentality at the crease reins supreme, the 27-year-old is the Test arena’s traditional throwback in the mould of his childhood idol, Mike Hussey. Building his game around solid defence on the front and back foot, while seeking low-risk scoring options, he has become the anchor of Queensland Sheffield Shield side since bursting onto the scene with a gutsy century on debut. That knock of 109 was the first instance in which he demonstrated his tendency for digging his team out of a slump. At one stage on that day in February 2022, the Bulls had slumped to 6–191, before Clayton’s defiance ground the Bulls to a first innings total of 349. His century in the 2024–25 Shield final was another instance of thriving in the pressure-cooker – combining with Jack Wildermuth (111) to overturn a 166 run first innings’ deficit to set South Australia 270 to win.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Clayton laughed “there are plenty of those moments I’ve stuffed up too”, but paid tribute to his first-grade coach Peter Clarke – now at the helm of the Sydney Sixers WBBL side – for shaping his mindset. “He was a sport psychologist for the Australian women’s team during that time, and he was really helpful for me in developing some processes around how I go about my cricket and how I compartmentalise things mentally,” Clayton explained. “I feel like that’s really helped me to make sure I stick to the process and focus on what I need to do in those situations to try and best help the team get into a position to win games.” Clayton’s call-up comes at a time when the Australian batting line-up has been hunting reinvention, culminating in the axing of Queensland teammate Marnus Labuschagne.

Advertisement

Despite spending much of his career batting at No.4, Clayton is poised to assume Labuschagne’s place at No.3; a challenge he will not shy away from, with his highest score of 134 coming in that same position last year. “I’d be happy to bat anywhere for Australia, one to 11 it wouldn’t bother me at all wherever I bat,” he quipped, before revealing the frank conversations he had with Labuschagne upon the latter’s return from the ill-fated tour in South Africa. “When he [Labuschagne] came back from South Africa, there was a bit of noise around me potentially taking his spot, but he was fantastic in the way he came up to me and talked about the elephant in the room straight away. Loading “He said ‘I don’t want any angst between us, I want the best for you, and I’m proud of all the stuff you’ve done and want you to be playing Test cricket and performing, and hopefully one day we can be there together’.’

Gruelling tours to India and England will follow the New Zealand battle in 2027, and there is no guarantee 37-year-old champion Steve Smith will play on beyond that. Clayton, however, was unwilling to contemplate a reality where he spearheaded the top order long-term. “As soon as you start thinking about those things in the future or things that you can’t control, I think that’s when I’ve had failures in my life. For me, it’ll be focusing on how I prepare for the first Test and how I can get myself in a situation to get out there and score runs,” Clayton said. “It won’t be going anything past the next training session, or the first session of day one, or whatever it is. title: A US sailor helped Julii's family flee Vietnam. Forty-four years later, they've reconnected
text:
IN BRIEF The Trinh family were recused by US sailors in the South China Sea after they fled Vietnam on an overcrowded boat.

After years of searching, Julii Trinh found one of the sailors, Jeff Carlson, through social media.

In 1982, Julii Trinh's parents made a life-changing decision — they fled Vietnam with their three young children aboard a small wooden boat carrying 83 people.

They dreamt of calling Australia home.

On 26 May 1982, after two days at sea, they were rescued by the crew of the USS Brewton.

Former US Navy sailor Jeff Carlson was part of the crew that rescued three-year-old Trinh and her family from the South China Sea.

Now, 44 years later, the pair have been reunited.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In a studio at SBS Melbourne, Trinh sits across from a screen, eagerly awaiting. When Carlson appears, emotion takes over.

"I'm good, I'm just in a bit of shock I think!" Trinh said.

"It's so nice to finally meet and chat with you. I know we've messaged, but to actually hear your voice. I just can't believe it. I'm lost for words."

When Trinh was growing up, her parents frequently reminded her how lucky they were to escape Vietnam and settle in Australia.

"Whenever I asked about how we came to Australia, they would simply say 'an American ship saved us'. That was all I knew," she told SBS Vietnamese.

"But as I got older, I became curious. I wanted to understand what led my parents to make that decision."

For Carlson, the memory of the day he pulled Trinh and her family to safety remains crystal clear.

He remembers being on watch and seeing a vessel overflowing with people bobbing in the ocean.

"It just seemed like it took so long before we actually saw the boat and started the rescue, getting everybody off. There was a lot of anxiety over that, especially when we could see through the binoculars how many kids were on board," he told SBS Vietnamese.

He said the crew carefully planned the rescue to ensure the safety of children on the boat.

Unlocking old memories

In 2014, Trinh's cousin who lives in the US found the USS Brewton yearbook online and sent her the link.

Inside were photographs of the rescue.

The discovery unlocked new information about her family's journey.

"I remember getting that email from my cousin. I clicked the link ... I saw this wooden boat rescue at sea, with a little story, and I thought, that's beautiful, that's amazing," she said.

"Then I clicked to the next page and all of a sudden I saw a picture of myself when I was very young.

Julii's parents and their grandchildren look at photos of the 1982 rescue in the South China Sea, preserved in the yearbook of the USS Brewton. Source: Supplied / Supplied by Julii Trinh

"As I turned the pages, there were more and more photos of me, then some of my family."

In shock, Trinh decided to print out the photographs and took them to her parents.

"They got really emotional, they were lost for words. I think that's when they were happy to open up and tell me more about it."

Finding Carlson on Facebook

Trinh tried tracking down the sailors involved in her rescue. But all her efforts failed.

This year, her father turned 75 — and the milestone prompted her to try again.

"I thought, what an amazing life he's had. I wanted to show him everything he sacrificed, from the decision he made that night to leave Vietnam, has allowed me and everyone around me to live the way we do," she said.

READ MORE Vietnamese refugee reunites with cargo ship rescuer

Trinh took to Facebook, finding a private group operating under the name of the USS Brewton 1086. Despite the rules stating those who weren't onboard and serving couldn't join, she tried anyway.

"I requested to join and got some questions I couldn't answer because they were secret code questions. But I wrote something like, 'I think I was one of the children that you rescued that night' and left it at that," she said.

"The next morning, I'd been accepted. I couldn't believe it."

Scrolling in the group, she saw a post marking the anniversary of her rescue.

"I commented, 'I was one of the children on that boat. I've always wondered where you were. I just want to say thank you. I can't believe it, and I just want to let you know that I've been living a very, very happy life.' Then there were a few comments from people who remembered that night, and it was very emotional," she said.

Images of the rescue on May 26, 1982, preserved in the USS Brewton's yearbook. Source: Supplied / Supplied by Julii Trinh

"They said it was one of the highlights of their deployment. They won the humanitarian service award that year. I was surprised that they remembered me."

One reply came from Carlson.

The pair chatted over social media for months. Now, they sit face-to-face over video link, and Carlson combs over his memories of the rescue.

"It was a big deal for a young man. Helping that many people, rescuing them from the South China Sea, was incredibly moving. I don't think anyone involved could ever forget it," he said.

"I'm proud of it, but I wasn't alone. I was just one sailor doing my job. There were many men involved in that rescue."

Julii speaks with former US Navy sailor Jeff Carlson via video link at the SBS Melbourne studio, 44 years after the rescue in the South China Sea. Source: SBS News / SBS Vietnamese

Carlson recalls the moment he connected with Trinh, and its impact on his life.

"When you found me, I was in a pretty dark place. Looking back on those years and sharing those memories with you helped me more than I can explain."

Carlson said his nickname for Trinh is 'Ray' — because he thinks of her like sunshine.

"You saved my life, and now I feel like I've been able to help pull you out of a dark place too," said Trinh.

A friendship that will last a lifetime

Trinh's feelings about the rescue have changed over the years — the biggest change came when she had her own children.

"If that was me, if I had to pick up my three children and run for my life, I just couldn't," she said.

"They were so brave. The courage they showed, for us to be here, I'm extremely grateful."

READ MORE The Vietnamese refugees who changed white Australia

Ending the call, Trinh says she spent years trying to imagine the men who rescued her family.

"My parents reminded us all the time that we were saved by an American ship. I often imagined the sailors, but they were only my imagination," she said.

"Now that I'm able to speak to you and see the photos, it means so much to me. I can't explain how much gratitude I have, and I will never forget you or this. Thank you."

"You're going to make me tear up. I didn't expect that," Carlson responded.

After 44 years of disconnection, the pair vowed to stay in touch and to build a friendship that will connect their families forever.

title: Labor shelves proposal to expand super for young workers despite internal support
text:
In brief Efforts to expand superannuation access for under-18 workers were shelved despite support from Labor's rank and file.

The decision leaves hundreds of thousands of young workers missing out on retirement savings.

Efforts to allow young workers to accrue retirement savings by opening up superannuation settings are to be quashed despite rank-and-file Labor support.

Underage employees are currently eligible for super only if they work more than 30 hours a week, meaning many under 18s with part-time jobs are denied contributions.

The Greens have led the push to remove the barrier during a parliamentary inquiry into the law, which has been around since the 1990s.

"(Some) 530,000 young workers are missing out on an estimated $411 million in superannuation contributions annually," Greens senator Barbara Pocock told the probe on Thursday.

Her comments came after committee chair and Labor senator Lisa Darmanin moved to shelve the reform.

Darmanin ultimately recommended the bill not be passed and suggested the proposal required consideration at a later date.

"The committee recognises that some of these reforms, particularly payday super, has required employers, payroll providers and superannuation to undertake significant and ongoing work to prepare for and implement the change," she noted in the final inquiry report.

That's despite Labor's members supporting extending the superannuation guarantee to under 18 employees at the party's national conference in Adelaide in July.

Opponents to the policy from the business sector have acknowledged the equity concerns it aimed to address but warned it would cripple employers after recent super reforms.

Tom Hughes, the incoming treasurer at the Australian National University Students' Association, said the exclusion of young workers from superannuation added to the broader hopelessness of getting ahead.

"For a system that we're so proud of to be entrenched within our working rights in Australia, for it to not be extended to young workers who do make up a considerable amount of the workforce ... is just not good enough," Hughes told the Australian Associated Press news agency.

"That entitlement shouldn't come from your status or your age. It should actually just come from the fact that you are working."

Despite the push from the Greens and the ensuing inquiry into scrapping the 30-hour threshold, the government did not support the move.

''This is now the third time Labor has refused to endorse this change in support of young workers, despite it being in its own Labor party policy platform," Pocock said.

Super Members Council chief executive Misha Schubert said she welcomed the government leaving the door open to further examination of the "unfair exclusion".

''When something is out of date, you fix it. It just makes sense that if you work, you should also be paid super, no matter how old you are,'' Schubert said in a statement.

title: Gadi Eisenkot accuses Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party of stalling Israeli government talks
text:
In brief Gadi Eisenkot has accused Benjamin Netanyahu's party of stalling coalition negotiations.

Efforts to form Israel's next government remained deadlocked.

Gadi Eisenkot, who is trying to form the next Israeli government, on Friday accused the party of caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections.

Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party has in recent days agreed coalition deals with two allied parties, but the route to a parliamentary majority is still far from certain.

After the October election failed to deliver a clear majority for either bloc, Yashar has also held talks with Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party over the possibility of forming a national unity government involving both parties.

But no breakthroughs on that front have ostensibly been reached.

"Likud, for its part, was unwilling to compromise and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table," Eisenkot said in a statement on Friday.

"Their conduct points to an effort to run down the clock until the mandate expires, split the Change bloc and drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government," he added.

Eisenkot has until 6 December — a deadline which can be extended by 14 days — to form a government to replace Netanyahu.

His wide-ranging camp has faced divisions on whether to forge alliances with the ultra-Orthodox parties, or the Arab-majority lists, or whether to form a unity government with Likud.

"We are approaching a moment of decision," Eisenkot said on Friday.

"The question is whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall," he added, but maintained he was still open to talks if Likud was "genuinely prepared to change course".

Likud, in turn, accused Eisenkot of working to form a "dangerous left-wing government" but nonetheless said it would still be open to a unity government.

Eisenkot's Yashar party has so far agreed coalition deals with the left-leaning Democrats party and the right-wing Israel Beiteinu party.

Together, they have a combined total of 36 lawmakers — far short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority.

On Friday, Israeli media reported that Mansour Abbas, the leader of the Arab-Israeli Raam party, was expected the following day to recognise Hamas as a "terror group" -- a move that could pave the way for his party to join a possible Eisenkot-led coalition.

But some of Eisenkot's allies have voiced opposition to relying on the support of the Arab-majority lists, which won unprecedented gains in the election.
