title: What happens when you privatise poo? Victoria could be about to find out
text:
In brief Experts say Jess Wilson's plan to sell management of Melbourne sewerage while maintaining public ownership is still privatisation.

One Nation, the Greens and Labor have all criticised the plan.

Two days before the Victorian election, state Opposition leader Jess Wilson unveiled a debt-reduction plan centred on the privatisation of swathes of land, renewable energy assets, air rights — and the leasing of the state's sewage treatment facilities.

The Coalition says a one-off $9.2 billion payment from a 90-year lease on Melbourne's sewerage would help fund a promised $20 billion reduction in net debt by 2030.

For close to a century, the Coalition will lease the Western Treatment Plant in Werribee, the Eastern Treatment Plant in Bangholme, nine pumping stations and 400km of sewerage beneath our streets.

The decision has drawn backlash from environmental groups and political parties, including the Greens and Labor, which earlier this year was revealed to have abandoned pursuit of a similar idea led by former premiers Daniel Andrews and Jacinta Allan.

Professor Monzur Imteaz, an environmental engineering expert at Swinburne University, said transferring operation of Melbourne's two largest sewage facilities to commercial operators could deliver prompt, dependable service for two reasons: because private firms "usually" escape the red tape that slows public agencies, and because fresh capital could fund modern, higher-performing technology.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

However, he told SBS News: "Upgraded infrastructure carries a price, and households would probably shoulder it through higher charges."

Imteaz said the Opposition is yet to explain how it would "restrain those escalations".

READ MORE The election surprise One Nation didn’t see coming

On Thursday, Wilson said the Essential Services Commission would continue to regulate water prices following the lease.

But Munirul Nabin, a senior lecturer in economics at Deakin University, said the arrangement warranted serious consideration.

"In economic terms, the Coalition is proposing giving operational control to a profit-motivated private company, under government price regulation," Nabin told SBS News.

"A private operator will always have a profit motive. That's not necessarily a bad thing, but if the government also caps prices, it can create distortions."

If a private company has exclusive operating rights for 90 years, it effectively becomes a monopoly operator, he said, adding that "the issue isn't ownership", but "who holds the power".

And if something were to go wrong, such as a natural disaster or drought, the private operator would have significant renegotiating power.

"People are already struggling with rising living costs and higher utility bills, and if a profit-motivated operator takes over, I believe prices will eventually increase one way or another."

Is a 90-year lease privatisation?

The Coalition took plans to privatise Melbourne Water to the 2018 and 2022 elections, but Wilson ruled it out earlier this year.

"We're not touching it," she told ABC News.

On Thursday, she argued the proposal was not privatisation because ownership would remain with the state.

"We're not privatising Melbourne Water. What we are doing is offering a 90-year lease for the sewerage assets to bring the interest bill down in this state."

Graeme Hodge, a privatisation and regulation expert and emeritus professor of law at Monash University, said this distinction was "nonsense".

"Calling a 90-year lease 'not privatisation' is, in my view, nonsense. That's political gameplay," he told SBS News.

"If you hand over the use of assets for 90 years, or 99 years as they do in places like Hong Kong and Saudi Arabia, then of course it's a privatisation."

Nabin agreed that in economic terms, "handing over operational control for three generations is functionally similar to privatisation", and warned the model created tensions between profit incentives and price regulation.

"Reducing debt is important, but any plan needs to address both the short- and long-term consequences," he said, adding that the policy was short-sighted.

Environmental concerns

The Victorian Greens and Labor have pointed to the United Kingdom as an example of the potential consequences of privatising water management.

Britain privatised its water sector in 1989. Since then, household bills have risen faster than inflation and regulators have faced criticism over sewage pollution.

In 2022, the UK's Environmental Audit Committee warned in a submission to an inquiry into river health that water companies appeared to be dumping untreated or partially treated sewage in rivers regularly, and that the impact of wastewater from sewage treatment works and sewer overflows was preventing 36 per cent of water bodies from achieving good ecological status.

"What we learned from the UK is that it wasn't a very good privatisation. They didn't put sufficiently strong regulation in place to control the private companies involved, and people received poorer services as a result," Hodge said.

"Even now, decades later, they're still trying to get the balance right."

Environmental groups have expressed concern that the lease risks disastrous consequences for Melbourne’s environment, including internationally important wetlands that support migratory birds from across the globe.

Professor Richard Kingsford, a Biodiversity Council member and waterbird and wetland expert, said the Western Treatment Plant was one of Australia's most important sites for waterbirds.

"Melbourne Water carefully manages nutrient levels in treated sewage to protect the health of Port Phillip Bay," he said.

"Maintaining these internationally important wetlands requires considerable ecological expertise, ongoing investment and careful management, which is hard to reconcile with companies whose objective is profit."

Hodge said that while privatisation could "make a lot of sense" if assets are run poorly, are run down, or managed incompetently, "that's not Victoria's situation".

"Victoria has one of the cleanest water supplies in the world through Melbourne Water and an excellent sewage treatment system.

"So I'm disappointed that politicians feel the need to privatise it."

While it was "impossible to say" whether privatisation arrangements always fail or always succeed, "the biggest winners from privatisation are, firstly, governments that receive the cash, and secondly, investors, who on average do very well", Hodge said.

"Private investors are not stupid — they acquire assets at what they regard as a good price and work them hard to make profits for their shareholders."

On Friday, One Nation said it would not support the plan, with Victorian leader Warren Pickering saying it was "privatisation in all but name".

title: David Shoebridge says the Greens need to stop 'preaching'. He's also not ruling out UFOs
text:
Key Points: David Shoebridge is predicting a Victorian Greens surge while arguing One Nation lacks a clear agenda.

The Greens leader has framed inequality and wealth redistribution as central to the Greens' mission.

Greens leader David Shoebridge says one of his party’s biggest problems has been spending too much time telling voters what it thinks rather than listening to what they want.

In a wide-ranging interview with SBS News as federal parliament wrapped for the year on Friday, Shoebridge reflected on the future of the Greens, wealth inequality, the Victorian election, sanctions against Russia and even unidentified aerial phenomena.

Shoebridge became the Greens' sixth leader on 30 September in a rare contested ballot after Larissa Waters resigned due to ill health. He then declared the party was "here to replace" Labor, and "beat down One Nation" by filling what he described as a Labor "policy vacuum" to build a "progressive, positive mass movement".

Despite his rhetoric, the Greens negotiated deals with the Albanese government this week to pass online safety laws, increase taxes on trusts, and retain pensioners' private health insurance rebates, in exchange for concessions including bigger fines for tech companies and higher private jet fuel taxes.

Shoebridge said the Greens need to "do a better job of connecting with people who are under pressure".

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"[We need to be] listening to people struggling with rent, mortgages, power bills and the cost of food," Shoebridge told SBS News.

"Not preaching solutions at them."

'The 99 per cent' versus the 1 per cent

Shoebridge said addressing inequality is central to the Greens' policies.

"We can see that there’s increasing concentrations of wealth in the 1 per cent or a fraction of the 1 per cent and how the rest of society is being pretty much sold out on an almost routine basis by key decision-makers, not least the federal parliament," he said.

"We're not here to tell people why billionaires and multinational corporations must continue getting richer.

"We're here to shift wealth away from billionaires and into the pockets of Australians who need it for food, power bills and housing."

Shoebridge described discretionary trusts as "basically a rort for the ultra-wealthy" and "only a tiny fraction of small businesses" use them. However, business groups warn these changes will impose substantial restructuring costs on thousands of small and family businesses.

According to accountancy body CPA Australia, the compliance costs for families and businesses affected by the discretionary trust changes are between $2 billion and $3 billion for advice, plus $220 million to $600 million per year in ongoing costs.

Shoebridge said people with enormous wealth can effectively buy political influence; it's dangerous for democracy and the economy.

"When you base your politics on fundamental truths like that, people recognise it," he said.

"In some ways it's like saying the emperor has no clothes. People are relieved that somebody is finally talking about it."

A Victorian test against One Nation

The Greens' electoral strategy is to offer voters angry with the major parties a left-wing alternative to One Nation, which he believes offers "meanness, nastiness and having a go at your neighbour".

"This idea of a One Nation surge seems to have collided with reality, where people are trying to work out what One Nation actually stands for," he said.

Polling from the final Victorian Newspoll and Demos AU polls indicated support for One Nation had dropped to 16-18 per cent, down from 25 per cent in Wednesday's Resolve poll. However, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson received passionate and broad support in Victoria at several campaign events on Friday, on the eve of the state election.

The Greens leader said promises of cheaper groceries through publicly owned stores, free public transport and making wealthy people and companies "pay their fair share” led him to a confident prediction of a "Green surge" in the state election.

READ MORE The election surprise One Nation didn’t see coming

In the run-up to the state election, polling suggests the Greens may gain lower-house seats while One Nation will struggle to turn its support into strong results. One recent poll put both parties on 16 per cent of the primary vote; modelling suggests the Greens could gain two or three lower-house seats.

"For the first time, in what's becoming a four-way contest, voters are taking a serious look at what the Greens are offering," he said.

Sanctions: 'Messaging' without substance

Shoebridge also took aim at the government over sanctions enforcement.

An audit of Australia’s sanctions system by the Australian National Audit Office (ANAO), released on Wednesday, found about 80 per cent of the actions taken involved nothing more than warning letters.

The government has accepted the audit's recommendations and is working to strengthen enforcement.

"What the ANAO report shows is that we have a Labor government that’s all about messaging, and not about substance," Shoebridge said.

Shoebridge has repeatedly opposed Australia sending weapons or military aid to Ukraine unless it is authorised by the United Nations Security Council while backing humanitarian, financial, and civilian assistance as well as tougher sanctions on Russian oil.

Opposing sending weapons to Ukraine without a United Nations mandate has caused dozens of Greens members to quit the party, given Russia has a permanent seat and veto power on the UN Security Council, the Australian Financial Review reported on Friday.

When asked if the audit showing sanctions are not being enforced changes his view, Shoebridge said one of the best ways we can support the people of Ukraine is through significant humanitarian and civilian assistance.

"At the same time, we should cut off the flow of money to the Russian military," he said. "Roughly 40 per cent of Russia's budget comes from oil revenue, and this government refuses to close loopholes that allow Russian oil to be refined through third countries and then imported into Australia."

An open mind on UFOs

Former Greens senator Peter Whish-Wilson asked questions in Senate Estimates and other parliamentary forums about unidentified aerial phenomena, which have been under investigation by United States government agencies and others for more than 80 years.

Shoebridge said he used to say to Whish-Wilson that "as long as they're unidentified, they're in his portfolio".

"If they start making contact and they're friendly, then they'd move into foreign affairs," he said. "If they turn out to be hostile, we'd probably shift them into defence.

"So I think we're still at the first stage. Look at the evidence. Keep an open mind. There are lots of reports and witness accounts. Some of that evidence could support a number of different conclusions. At this stage, I simply have an open mind. I think it's foolish to look at the available information and declare with certainty that it's definitely one thing or another."

title: China's top officials are falling. Here's how the purge has unfolded
text:
IN BRIEF An investigation into Shanghai secretary Chen Jining is "particularly shocking", an analyst says.

It is part of sweeping expulsions in China's top brass.

Chinese President Xi Jinping's sweeping anti-corruption campaign has claimed some of the country's most powerful political and military figures, reshaping the leadership ranks of the Communist Party and removing officials once considered untouchable.

Supporters say the drive has strengthened party discipline and public trust, while critics argue it has also helped Xi consolidate power ahead of a key party congress expected in 2027.

The campaign escalated again this week when China's anti-corruption watchdog announced an investigation into Politburo member and Shanghai party secretary Chen Jining, one of the country's most senior civilian officials.

Chen, 62, is accused of "suspected severe violations of discipline and laws", a phrase commonly used by Chinese authorities to refer to corruption and other political offences.

The investigation follows the purge of three other members of the elite leadership body, which was formed in 2022 with 24 members.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Now, with Chen under investigation, there are 21 acting members — China's Central Military Commission (CMC) vice chair Zhang Shengmin was promoted to the body last month.

Chen, a UK-educated environmental scientist, was appointed environmental protection minister in 2015, before becoming Beijing's mayor. In 2022, he joined the Politburo in the party's chief position in Shanghai.

The position is part of a well-trodden path to the party's top leadership post — once being held by both current President Xi Jinping and former president Jiang Zemin.

Wen-Ti Sung, a nonresident fellow at the Atlantic Council's Global China Hub, told the Reuters news agency Chen's investigation is "particularly shocking".

"Chen's purge is particularly shocking in that he poses no military threat, and doesn't deviate from Xi on major symbolic issues like ethnic policy," Sung said, referring to Xi's emphasis on integration into mainstream Chinese culture.

"But he got purged anyway, so far without even an explanation. The shock is bound to reverberate."

Chen Jining, Party Secretary of Shanghai and member of Politburo, is being investigated for corruption. Source: AFP / Adek Berry

China expert Jean ⁠Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich said Chen's probe "sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the Party’s 'self-revolution'".

"If anything, it continues to intensify," he told Reuters.

Millions of CCP members and officials have been caught up in Xi's anti-graft campaign that has now been running for 14 years.

Recently, a record 33 dignitaries were expelled when the CCP's powerful Central Committee gathered. It came as the 21st Party Congress was for the second half of 2027 , effectively starting proceedings for China's tightly choreographed, twice-a-decade top reshuffle, when Xi is expected to extend his rule for another five-year term.

The party's fifth plenum saw leaders place political loyalty front and centre, as they vowed to keep purging 'impurities and viruses' from party ranks ahead of next year's congress.

Xi is "clearing the ground" before next year's gathering, sweeping aside entrenched political customs and older networks to build a more ideologically aligned leadership lineup, a senior Asian diplomat said.

The Central Committee, "with comrade Xi Jinping at its core", has "eliminated serious hidden dangers within the party, the state and the military," Zhang Fuhai, deputy secretary of the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, said on Friday.

The party, he told reporters at a news briefing, had been guided by the sense of mission that "we would rather offend thousands than let down 1.4 billion people", referring to China's population.

Three major officials expelled

Chen is the fourth Politburo member investigated in just over a year as the anti-corruption drive reaches the CCP's innermost circle, having already ensnared Central Military Commission vice chairmen Zhang Youxia and He Weidong, as well as former Xinjiang party chief Ma Xingrui.

Ma left his post as Xinjiang party chief in July 2025 and has been absent from public view since appearing at a major party meeting in October last year.

His investigation was publicly announced in April. He was accused of "serious violations of law and discipline" and expelled from the party in July — weeks after his dismissal from the National People's Congress.

Ma Xingrui was indicted on bribery charges in November. Source: AFP / Greg Baker

Ma was accused of large-scale "family corruption" and seeking benefits from others in the appointment of officials and improper job arrangements. The country's anti-corruption watchdog said he helped relatives purchase property at below-market prices and engaged in exchanges involving power and money for sex.

In November, China's top prosecuting agency indicted Ma on bribery charges.

Ma began his career in regional politics in the affluent southern province of Guangdong.

He had also served at the China National Space Administration and was vice minister of the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

Zhang was placed under probe in January and then removed from the CMC in August.

The former first-ranked vice-chairman of the CMC was accused of disloyalty to the party and of abandoning party principles, as well as of corrupt self-enrichment and abuse of office.

Analysts said the corruption charges were not unusual, but the allegations of disloyalty, including forming cliques and factions, were unusually explicit.

Zhang was one of the few leading officers with combat experience, whose father had fought in the civil war alongside Xi's father.

China's Central Military Commission Vice President Zhang Youxia was removed from office in August 2026. Source: AFP / Ichiro Ohara/The Yomiuri Shimbun

He Weidong was removed as Vice Chairman of the CMC and Politburo member, and expelled from the Chinese Communist Party and the People's Liberation Army on 17 October, 2025.

The defence ministry said he was expelled over serious party discipline violations and suspected of serious duty-related crimes involving an "exceptionally large amount of money".

His expulsion made him the first serving uniformed Central Military Commission vice-chair to be removed since the 1966-1976 Cultural Revolution.

— With additional reporting by the Agence France-Presse and Reuters news agencies.

title: Passport information may have been exposed in Flight Centre cyber incident
text:
In brief Flight Centre is investigating a data breach that may have exposed some customer information.

The incident has raised concerns about passport details and travel records being accessed.

Travel giant Flight Centre is investigating a data breach at one of its booking providers which may have exposed customer passport information.

The company is investigating "unusual activity" in a third-party accommodation booking system used by its brands, it said in a statement to the ASX on Thursday.

"[Flight Centre] is still working with the third-party vendor and [our] cybersecurity incident response partner ... to understand the nature and extent of the activity," the statement said.

Flight bookings and corporate travel bookings were not affected, the company said.

A significant number of customer records are believed to have been accessed by unknown persons, but the company said it did not know how many records had actually been extracted.

title: Plan to keep more Australian gas onshore set to become law after Labor, Coalition form deal
text:
In brief Labor had convinced the Coalition to strike a deal on its domestic gas reservation scheme.

It is hoped the scheme will deliver a "modest oversupply" of gas from 2028.

The Coalition agreed to pass Labor's domestic gas reservation scheme, despite concerns, on Thursday afternoon.

The policy forces liquefied natural gas (LNG) exporters to set aside up to 20 per cent of their supply for the Australian market, starting in 2028.

This is expected to generate a "modest oversupply" of gas and push down prices, the government has previously said.

The Australian Energy Regulator will forecast domestic demand, add a 10 per cent market oversupply buffer, subtract non-exporter supply, and spread the remaining amount across LNG exporters.

A provision to exclude Western Australia has been broadly agreed, but the details are yet to be decided.

title: 'The costs are enormous': Behind some Australians' front doors is a $3.8 billion burden
text:
In brief A new report has described Australia's housing crunch as a public health crisis.

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

When housing and public health researcher Rebecca Bentley asks a room full of people if they've ever lived in a home with mould, she tends to get a similar response: most raise their hands.

"We do actually have a high tolerance for mould and damp in Australian homes because it's something we've grown to accept a bit," the University of Melbourne professor told SBS News.

But experts say that tolerance comes at a cost.

New research led by the university's Healthy Housing Unit estimates that eliminating household mould could save Australia $3.8 billion in healthcare expenditure and prevent $5.9 billion in lost income over the next 20 years.

And mould isn't the only hazard that could be harming Australians inside their own homes.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The research estimates that 2.5 million Australian households live in unhealthy homes, with issues such as poor ventilation, exposure to pollutants and toxins, pests and extreme indoor temperatures posing risks to occupants' health.

Its authors say high housing prices are pushing Australians into homes that don't meet their needs, with renters more likely to be exposed to poor-quality homes.

"We know that there's an affordability crisis in Australia. That housing supply is low. Rental affordability is not good in Australia at the moment," said Bentley, who is also director of the Centre of Research Excellence in Healthy Housing.

"So all of these things contribute to this large burden of what we would describe as unhealthy housing in Australia."

How can unhealthy housing affect people?

Poor housing conditions can contribute to respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses and poor mental health, as well as affect children's development, productivity and life expectancy.

Bentley said the health consequences of household mould extend beyond physical conditions such as asthma, with exposure also taking a toll on people's mental health — something that was not factored into the modelling.

"So in fact, this estimate of $3.8 billion is actually a relatively conservative estimate," she said.

Distinguished professor Brian Oliver, who researches environmental health at the University of Technology Sydney, said the economic burden of household mould alone might surprise people.

"Even minor ailments cost money.

"It's not like if you've got mould in your bathroom, you're going to drop dead. But if you feel unwell, if you've got days off work, if you're visiting a healthcare practitioner, and if you've got chronic exposure and it leads to chronic disease, then the costs are enormous."

Some housing-related hazards are less visible, such as exposure to excessive noise.

Oliver said noise from busy roads or nearby industrial activity can disrupt residents' sleep, with long-term sleep deprivation linked to a range of health problems.

Living near busy roads can also affect the quality of the air residents breathe.

"Some people live next to busy roads, and they may as well be camping on the road because of the way that their houses work," Oliver told SBS News.

Recognising when your home is making you sick

Oliver said one potential indication that a person's home is affecting their health is if their symptoms improve when they spend time away from it.

He said it's also worth paying attention if a guest observes something about your home that you may have grown accustomed to.

"If you have someone come into your house, and they say, 'Oh, there's an unusual smell', or 'I don't feel so well', that's something you should definitely take notice of."

However, Oliver cautioned against becoming overly concerned about minor exposure to household hazards, noting that the level of exposure matters.

He said there are simple steps people can take to improve the health of their homes, such as opening a bathroom window or switching on an extractor fan after showering to reduce moisture build-up.

If you suspect your home is affecting your health, Oliver recommends speaking to a GP.

What can be done about unhealthy housing?

The report's authors say improving housing quality could save the country money and improve Australians' quality of life.

In particular, the report calls for stronger and more consistent protections for renters nationally, including minimum housing standards covering ventilation, indoor temperatures, repairs, mould and damp.

Roughly a third of the Australian population is renting, and that share is expected to expand over time.

"If renters don't feel like they will be evicted or their rent will be put up if they say ask for mould to be fixed in their home, that's another way in which we can just increase the probability that these problems will be addressed and reduced for people," Bentley said.

The report also calls for stronger construction regulations to improve the quality of new homes, including measures to reduce exposure to environmental noise and extreme indoor temperatures and minimise maintenance issues.

"The choice before us is clear. We can continue to meet the costs of unhealthy housing through hospitals, welfare systems, lost productivity and preventable suffering," Bentley said.

"Or we can invest upstream — in homes that keep people healthy, safe and secure."

A two-storey art deco East Lindfield home passed in at auction with a vendor’s bid of $3.2 million on Saturday. Staff from real estate agency DiJones almost outnumbered bidders and onlookers as they stood in the front garden of 82 Tryon Road, with both registered bidders arriving just minutes before the auction for the four-bedroom property began. The property was one of 1073 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 42 per cent from 637 reported results throughout the week, while 278 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. After extolling its original features spanning patterned ceilings, sandstone paving, and a curved stairwell with metal balustrade, auctioneer Josh Larsen opened bidding on the East Lindfield home.

Advertisement

Despite several conversations among sales agents and bidders, no one could be convinced to place a bid. After 10 minutes, the property passed in and the auction ended. Related Article Property prices The most liveable, affordable suburbs for property buyers At the time of publication, the property, which had a guide of $3 million and a reserve of $3.4 million, had not sold. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. The house, which has covered terraces, parking for two cars and a studio space on the lower ground floor, was offered for the first time in more than 35 years.

Advertisement

Record show it last sold in 1991 for $470,000. It was the vendors’ family home, but they have held it as an investment since moving to the north coast. There was plenty of room to move at the auction of 82 Tryon Road, but it was not enough to entice bidders to raise their paddles. Sitthixay Ditthavong Larsen said while he had seen an uptick in transactions in the past eight weeks, the result reflected ongoing hesitation among buyers. “We have two very interested parties here, and we are trying to see what we can do,” he said. “We are seeing some engagement, but buyers are cautious.” The house still has many of its original features including patterned ceilings and a double archway leading to french doors. Domain

Advertisement

Earlier in the week, sales agent for DiJones, Nahid Coventry was anticipating strong interest from three parties, but only two showed up on the day, with buyers “hedging their bets” in the current market. “People are nervous,” she said. “They are still waiting to see rock bottom. Everyone is out for a bargain.” In Balmain, a three-storey, four-bedroom home sold for $4,402,000 at auction on Saturday, $352,000 over the reserve to a family from Ryde. Six parties registered to bid for 26 Birchgrove Road, with four active. Bidding opened at $3.75 million, $25,000 below the $4 million guide. The property called “Riverview” has scenic water views alongside a split-level garden deck and pool.

Advertisement

After the first couple of bids of $25,000 increments, the increments then jumped around from $5000 to $10,000 to $1000 bids. In the final moments it got down to increments of $1000 and $500, before the hammer fell and the property sold. It had a reserve of $4,050,000. The successful bidders were a family with teenagers from Ryde who were not present, but had a buyer’s agent acting on their behalf. They were attracted by the two living areas and swimming pool the house offered. The underbidders were an inner west family with three young children, while the vendors were relocating to Melbourne. A family from Ryde are all set for summer with the purchase of a four-bedroom home in Balmain. Domain

Advertisement

Belle Property Balmain sales agent, Monique Dower, said the house was last renovated about 16 years ago but had been refreshed ahead of the sale. “A lot of money was spent on the presentation to bring it up to a certain standard, including new carpets, new floors and a garden upgrade”. Records show the home last sold in 2008 for $1,535,000. Related Article Housing affordability Why the property downturn hasn’t made it much easier to buy a home In Sylvania, a single level, four-bedroom home sold for $2,155,000 to a couple from Zetland who paid $45,000 below reserve. They were moving to be closer to family.

Ten parties registered to vie for the keys to 21 Endeavour Street, with four active. Bidding opened with an offer of $1.9 million, followed by two further increments of $50,000. When bidding reached $2.1 million, which was also the guide, activity stalled. Sales agent for McGrath Sylvania, Bill Tsounias, then negotiated with the leading bidder to increase their offer to $2,155,000 and the hammer fell. The property had a reserve of $2.2 million. 21 Endeavour Street comes complete with a pool and cabana, ready for summer. Domain

Advertisement

The underbidders were a couple from Beverley Park who had sold their home last weekend. The vendors were taking advantage of market conditions to buy a larger home. Tsounias said the turnkey nature of the property was appealing to buyers, but not enough for most to raise their paddles. “[Results like this] clearly show that [you can have] 10 bidders but the second you hit the price guide, you have two bidders,” he said. “You tell them exactly where [the pricing] will be, and they still rock up thinking it might go for well under.”

Unheralded German Nicolai Von Dellingshausen has a Ryder Cup winner snapping at his heels as he eyes the biggest victory of his career at the Australian PGA and a potential major championship debut. In windy conditions that blew Von Dellinghausen’s playing partner Cameron Smith off course at The Lakes Golf Club in Sydney, the world No.333 took a three-shot lead through 54 holes at 16 under par. Nicolai Von Dellingshausen tees off at the Australian PGA Championship on Saturday. Getty Images Von Dellingshausen carded a gutsy 69 and continued to upstage several big names including Smith, Adam Scott and Min Woo Lee. In their place, 12-time DP World Tour winner and world No.25 Alex Noren threw his hat into the ring with a bogey-free 65 to climb to outright second at 13 under par.

Advertisement

“I’m extremely happy about the last two days,” world No.25 Noren, a member of Europe’s 2018 Ryder Cup-winning team, said after seven birdies on day three. “[The Lakes] varies and gives you opportunities when you have to step up. I took care of the par 5s and then you can play some of the other holes a little bit more defensively. It’s a really fun course to play.” Noren and Von Dellingshausen will comprise the final group on Sunday, teeing off at 12.15pm. Sweden’s Alex Noren moved into second place on Saturday. Getty Images Two-time Australian PGA champion Scott climbed to nine under with a bogey-free 65 that included an eagle at the par-5 eighth. At seven shots behind the lead, former world No.1 Scott gave himself a green light for an aggressive final round on Sunday. “I think I should, because what difference does it make?” Scott said. “I’m really in a fortunate position. I think I’ve won [it] twice before, so it’s not like I’m protecting anything. I should just have a crack.”

Advertisement

In front of large Sydney galleries cheering on Smith, the 2022 British Open winner struggled in the breeze to a two-over 74 that dropped his total to seven under. The third member of the group, Northern Ireland’s Tom McKibbin, missed a short birdie putt on the 17th but a solid 70 kept him within four shots of the lead. Off day: Cameron Smith. Getty Images Von Dellingshausen said he would spend the night either at his accommodation in Coogee with his wife and children, or exploring the Opera House with his mind coach to distract himself from what is at stake at the $2.5 million Australian PGA. The winner will be awarded a DP World Tour card for two years and more than $400,000 in prizemoney. But another significant carrot dangling is that, for the first time, the Australian PGA champion will receive a direct invitation to the US PGA Championship next year, one of golf’s four majors. “Yes, [winning] would [secure] my first major, which would be a huge thing,” Von Dellingshausen said. “At the same time, what I want to do is after the round, just look in the mirror and say, ‘Hey, I gave it my all and whatever happened, happened.’”

Advertisement

Von Dellingshausen would also have the rare honour of becoming the first German to have his name engraved on the Joe Kirkwood Cup in the almost 100-year history of the Australian PGA. His only DP World Tour victory to date was last year’s Austrian Open. “[This is] completely different,” he said. “I would say I’m a more complete player now than I was in Austria,

I was playing in front of home crowds back in Austria because it was very close to Germany. “I am going to be very nervous [on Sunday]. There’s a reason to be nervous and I did a good job today to really embrace it and to manage it. This is what I worked for. The best that I can do is just go out there, enjoy it tomorrow and hit shot by shot.”

Jack Clayton offers a chuckle and wry smile when asked to recall the moment which paved his way towards earning his Baggy Green. Cricket was not a career path he envisioned when the Brisbane Lions academy prospect pondered what missing selection in the AFL draft would mean. When he picked up the bat for the University of Queensland, he was playing third-grade and was reluctant to give up his Saturday mornings when a request to be promoted to the seconds was offered. Queensland’s Jack Clayton celebrating a Sheffield Shield century at the Gabba. Chris Hyde/Getty Images Nine years to the day when he went un-drafted, and he is on the cusp of becoming Australia’s 474th Test cricketer, having been named in the squad to face New Zealand in Perth from December 9. “I certainly never thought when I gave up my footy dream that I would be in this position nine years later. At that stage, I did think I was going to go back and play footy for that season,” Clayton said on Saturday.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Test cricket Power rankings: The quicks and spinners primed to succeed all-star Test attack “The next season, Scott Henry – our first-grade captain, who also played for New South Wales and Queensland – told me I was going to bat three for the season, and I fell flat on my face when he said that. It’s obviously been a bit of a different journey, but one I’m really proud of.” That call-up marked a sliding doors moment for Clayton, who had initially intended to attempt an AFL revival mission through the NEAFL – now the VFL – with Aspley Hornets. “I think being out of that professional set-up with footy … and just being a normal 18, 19, 20-year-old going through uni, hanging out with mates, doing all the things uni people do, gave me a lot of perspective about life, but also where sport lies in my life,” he said. “I feel like that’s helped keep me balanced and level throughout my cricket career.”

Advertisement

While fellow Test contenders Sam Konstas and Jake Weatherald have fought for re-inclusion in the spotlight, Clayton has been able to slowly hone his craft free of scrutiny. In an era where T20 cricket and the smash and bash mentality at the crease reins supreme, the 27-year-old is the Test arena’s traditional throwback in the mould of his childhood idol, Mike Hussey. Building his game around solid defence on the front and back foot, while seeking low-risk scoring options, he has become the anchor of Queensland Sheffield Shield side since bursting onto the scene with a gutsy century on debut. That knock of 109 was the first instance in which he demonstrated his tendency for digging his team out of a slump. At one stage on that day in February 2022, the Bulls had slumped to 6–191, before Clayton’s defiance ground the Bulls to a first innings total of 349. His century in the 2024–25 Shield final was another instance of thriving in the pressure-cooker – combining with Jack Wildermuth (111) to overturn a 166 run first innings’ deficit to set South Australia 270 to win.

Advertisement

Related Article Updated

Australian cricket Lyon weighing up playing future after Test snub as replacement revealed Clayton laughed “there are plenty of those moments I’ve stuffed up too”, but paid tribute to his first-grade coach Peter Clarke – now at the helm of the Sydney Sixers WBBL side – for shaping his mindset. “He was a sport psychologist for the Australian women’s team during that time, and he was really helpful for me in developing some processes around how I go about my cricket and how I compartmentalise things mentally,” Clayton explained. “I feel like that’s really helped me to make sure I stick to the process and focus on what I need to do in those situations to try and best help the team get into a position to win games.” Clayton’s call-up comes at a time when the Australian batting line-up has been hunting reinvention, culminating in the axing of Queensland teammate Marnus Labuschagne.

Advertisement

Despite spending much of his career batting at No.4, Clayton is poised to assume Labuschagne’s place at No.3; a challenge he will not shy away from, with his highest score of 134 coming in that same position last year. “I’d be happy to bat anywhere for Australia, one to 11 it wouldn’t bother me at all wherever I bat,” he quipped, before revealing the frank conversations he had with Labuschagne upon the latter’s return from the ill-fated tour in South Africa. “When he [Labuschagne] came back from South Africa, there was a bit of noise around me potentially taking his spot, but he was fantastic in the way he came up to me and talked about the elephant in the room straight away. Loading “He said ‘I don’t want any angst between us, I want the best for you, and I’m proud of all the stuff you’ve done and want you to be playing Test cricket and performing, and hopefully one day we can be there together’.’

Advertisement

Gruelling tours to India and England will follow the New Zealand battle in 2027, and there is no guarantee 37-year-old champion Steve Smith will play on beyond that. Clayton, however, was unwilling to contemplate a reality where he spearheaded the top order long-term. “As soon as you start thinking about those things in the future or things that you can’t control, I think that’s when I’ve had failures in my life. For me, it’ll be focusing on how I prepare for the first Test and how I can get myself in a situation to get out there and score runs,” Clayton said. “It won’t be going anything past the next training session, or the first session of day one, or whatever it is. I try and keep it as simple as I can in that sense, and not look too far forward in the future, and just focus on what I can do and what I can control. “What I’ve been doing in Shield cricket has been working against good quality first-class bowlers, and even international bowlers, so I’m not changing anything about the way I prepare.” Sports news, results and expert commentary. title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years

Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.
